newsitem.title: CROATIA: Political woes mount for Croatia's Tudjman.
newsitem.headline: Political woes mount for Croatia's Tudjman.

text.p: Political woes mounted for Croatia's ailing President Franjo Tudjman on Wednesday as public sector workers demonstrated against austerity and a supreme court judge contested his sacking on sex charges.
Unrest grew as doubts swirled round Tudjman's own future after sources in the United States, where he has undergone medical treatment, claimed he had cancer.
The official Croatian version is that the president, who led Croatia to independence from former Yugoslavia in 1991, is suffering from digestive problems.
Around 1,000 public employees including school and university teachers marched in Zagreb on Wednesday in support of demands for 50 per cent salary increases which the government has rejected.
Labour unrest was uncommon in Croatia despite an austerity drive that has impoverished workers in an economy damaged by four years of war that followed its secession.
But wood-processing workers in the Adriatic port of Rijeka led the way in October with protests for higher wages and better social benefits.
More than 5,000 pensioners, whose monthly incomes average $150 a month rallied last Saturday in support of demands for "a dignified life". Rail workers scheduled a general strike for Thursday.

The largest rally in years came a week ago, when an attempt by Tudjman's nationalist government to close down independent Radio 101, a symbol of free speech to many Croats, mobilised 100,000 protestors at Zagreb's main square.
The rally grew into a wider call for more democracy as opposition leaders took the stage and delivered fiery speeches against the ruling HDZ party's alleged abuse of power.
The radio dispute occurred while Tudjman was being treated in Washington and he came back determined to dispel claims that he had only a year to live.
On his return to Zagreb he gave a news conference where he alternately smiled and banged his fist to prove his vigour.
Observers believe the 74-year-old president will run again in 1997 presidential elections, despite the declining popularity of his nationalist HDZ party.
Acting on instructions from the government, the National Judicial Council on Tuesday suspended the head of the supreme court, Krunislav Olujic, accusing him of paedophilia.

Olujic replied on Wednesday that the Council's decision was illegal and politically motivated. "This damages the constitutional principle of independence of courts," he said in a statement carried by the state news agency HINA.
